title: Strength: Using Your Energy to Steady Yourself

quickTake.upright: Keep your temper and find your courage. A gentler approach can still get things done.
quickTake.reversed: Pushing harder is making things more strained. Are you forcing yourself onward or trying to overpower someone?

hook: A strong person can also soften their movements. Under pressure, this card asks how you use your strength.

sections.title: Look at Her Hands, Then the Lion's Body
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Against a broad yellow background, a woman in white bends toward an orange-red lion. She wears a floral crown, and a garland at her waist falls beside its mane. A horizontal figure-eight symbol hangs above her head. One hand rests near the lion's upper jaw and the other supports its lower jaw; neither arm is raised to strike. The lion lifts its head, mouth open and tongue visible, with its tail curling between its hind legs and all four paws still on the ground.

She wears no armor, and the image contains no weapon. Her clothes fall vertically, while the lion's body extends horizontally; stillness and movement meet at the contact of her hands. Behind them are grass, shrubs, and a blue mountain, with a fairly open view. Retain these visible relationships before naming the action. The still image alone cannot prove whether she is opening or closing the lion's mouth. [View the card image used in this article](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:RWS_Tarot_08_Strength.jpg)

Both hands are close to the mouth; the woman is not directing the animal from far away. This close contact can suggest to modern readers that responding to a strong reaction begins with seeing clearly how it is unfolding. The garland and unarmored body also make the picture's strength something more than force meeting force. Yet this is a symbolic image, absolutely not a demonstration of how to approach a real predator. Nor can it require someone under threat to change another person through gentleness. In a life situation, locate “steadiness” in actions you can choose: pausing before a hurtful reply, for example, and then stating a boundary clearly.

sections.title: Waite's Strength Has a Religious Background
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Waite explicitly describes the action as closing the lion's mouth and explains that the lion has been subdued by beneficent fortitude, while the flower chain carries the symbolism of divine law. He connects one aspect of the lion with passions and specifically distinguishes his religious form of confidence from ordinary self-confidence. Reducing the card to “believe in yourself and you will succeed” loses the original context. [Waite, Part II, VIII](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktar08.htm)

The discussion of emotion and action below is this site's reflective reading for contemporary life. It also does not turn the figures' genders into rules about who must be gentle or who needs taming.

sections.title: Upright: Giving Courage a Concrete Action
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Upright can mean that something is difficult and you can still remain clear-headed and keep doing what needs doing. Anger may alert you to a crossed boundary; fear may show that something matters. Identify the feeling before choosing a response, and strength gains a direction.

Gentleness can also be firm. Clearly saying “I can't meet this request” is different from repeatedly yielding. If you are already exhausted, seeking support and reducing the task can likewise preserve your ability to act.

sections.title: Reversed: Notice Both Ends of the Imbalance
sections.bodyMarkdown: Reversal can be examined at two ends: continually trying to control things through urging, blame, or bravado, and becoming so depleted that even expressing a need feels beyond you. Waite's old list contains both abuse of power and weakness, already suggesting these possibilities. This site further recommends examining triggers and workload rather than labeling yourself “not strong enough.” [Waite, Part III, §3, entry 8](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pkt0303.htm)

sections.title: Distinguishing Related Meanings
sections.bodyMarkdown: Strength and the Emperor can both address boundaries. The Emperor can clarify responsibilities and systems; Strength pays more attention to enforcing a boundary without being driven by a passing emotion. It also differs from Temperance: Temperance adjusts an overall balance, whereas Strength can happen in a brief instant when you are already angry but still have a choice about what to say. Reversal cannot simply mean weak will. Sometimes sustained strain has reduced available energy; sometimes controlling others has been mistaken for personal strength. Look at specific behavior, not a personality label assigned by one card.

sections.title: Responding After Being Criticized in Public
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Xufan asks, “A friend made fun of my work in front of everyone. How should I respond?”

Known facts: He heard an explicitly belittling joke and felt very angry. His friend has previously accepted serious feedback from him, but they have not discussed this incident. Xufan fears that once he begins speaking, all his accumulated frustrations will spill out. He draws upright Strength in the advice position.

The woman's hands near the lion's mouth, without striking it, can inspire translating intense feelings into controllable expression. This does not require Xufan to suppress anger or treat the other person as a lion waiting to be tamed. What he can choose is the timing, wording, and way of leaving the conversation. Upright suits acknowledging hurt while giving a boundary a clear form.

Another possibility: If there have already been threats, sustained humiliation, or retaliation, face-to-face persuasion should not be the first choice; safety and support come first. If memories of the joke differ, first check the actual words rather than treating inference as fact.

A practical next step: Write down exactly what was said, its effect, and what he wants in future. Choose a calm private moment to say, “I'm not okay with my work being joked about like that,” and observe whether the friend is willing to adjust. If the boundary is crossed again, he can end that exchange without arguing until he wins.

sections.title: When Every Practice Session Is a Struggle, Where Does Patience Come From?
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Xiaoman asks, “Whenever I make a mistake in choir practice, I blame myself. How can I become steadier?”

Known facts: Her practice sessions keep getting longer, but she often repeats the same passage while exhausted. Her teacher has said she knows the correct way to sing it, yet rushes to restart after a mistake and gets more confused the more she hurries. She draws reversed Strength in the obstacle position.

Here, reversal fits excessive force more than lack of ability. The lion's strong vitality can represent the impulse to correct an error immediately. The woman's steady posture suggests allowing one mistake before choosing an action. The known teaching feedback supports an existing foundation. Accelerating through self-blame may instead conceal precisely which beat went wrong.

Another possibility: If she has not actually understood the melody or vocal requirement, she needs another demonstration from her teacher; a technical issue should not all be called an emotional one. If practice is affecting everyday functioning, reducing the load and seeking suitable support are also worth considering.

A practical next step: Reduce the difficult passage to two bars. After an error, stop, listen, mark its location, then repeat slowly. Set an endpoint for practice and record accuracy rather than how often she blames herself. Bring the most frequent trouble spot to her teacher next time to see whether the adjustment really helps.

sections.title: Practice: Give Your Energy a Place to Go
sections.bodyMarkdown: Write about a recent moment when you nearly lost control, in three lines: what I felt; what I wanted to protect; and one specific sentence I could use next time to express a boundary. Practice one sentence, such as “I'm willing to deal with this, but I need until tomorrow to answer.”

sections.title: A Common Misreading
sections.bodyMarkdown: Strength does not mean never getting angry or becoming nobler the longer you endure. The pictured contact can help you think about regulation and courage, but cannot prove anyone naturally strong or weak, or decide how much you should tolerate.

articleMarkdown:
# Strength: Using Your Energy to Steady Yourself

Upright in a sentence: Keep your temper and find your courage. A gentler approach can still get things done.

Reversed in a sentence: Pushing harder is making things more strained. Are you forcing yourself onward or trying to overpower someone?

A strong person can also soften their movements. Under pressure, this card asks how you use your strength.

## Look at Her Hands, Then the Lion's Body

## Upright: Giving Courage a Concrete Action

Upright can mean that something is difficult and you can still remain clear-headed and keep doing what needs doing. Anger may alert you to a crossed boundary; fear may show that something matters. Identify the feeling before choosing a response, and strength gains a direction.

Gentleness can also be firm. Clearly saying “I can't meet this request” is different from repeatedly yielding. If you are already exhausted, seeking support and reducing the task can likewise preserve your ability to act.

## Reversed: Notice Both Ends of the Imbalance

Reversal can be examined at two ends: continually trying to control things through urging, blame, or bravado, and becoming so depleted that even expressing a need feels beyond you. Waite's old list contains both abuse of power and weakness, already suggesting these possibilities. This site further recommends examining triggers and workload rather than labeling yourself “not strong enough.” [Waite, Part III, §3, entry 8](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pkt0303.htm)

## Distinguishing Related Meanings

Strength and the Emperor can both address boundaries. The Emperor can clarify responsibilities and systems; Strength pays more attention to enforcing a boundary without being driven by a passing emotion. It also differs from Temperance: Temperance adjusts an overall balance, whereas Strength can happen in a brief instant when you are already angry but still have a choice about what to say. Reversal cannot simply mean weak will. Sometimes sustained strain has reduced available energy; sometimes controlling others has been mistaken for personal strength. Look at specific behavior, not a personality label assigned by one card.

## Responding After Being Criticized in Public
